# The pro-regenerative effects of hyperIL6 in drug-induced liver injury are unexpectedly due to competitive inhibition of IL11 signaling

## Authors

- Jinrui Dong<sup>1</sup>
- Sivakumar Viswanathan<sup>1</sup>
- Eleonora Adami<sup>1</sup>
- Sebastian Schafer<sup>1</sup>
- Fathima F Kuthubudeen<sup>1</sup>
- Anissa A Widjaja<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0001-9404-7608](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9404-7608))
- Stuart A Cook<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0001-6628-194X](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6628-194X)) †

3. MRC-London Institute of Medical Sciences, Hammersmith Hospital Campus London United Kingdom

## Abstract

It is generally accepted that IL6-mediated STAT3 signaling in hepatocytes, mediated via glycoprotein 130 (gp130; IL6ST), is beneficial and that the synthetic IL6:IL6ST fusion protein (HyperIL6) promotes liver regeneration. Recently, autocrine IL11 activity that also acts via IL6ST but uses ERK rather than STAT3 to signal, was found to be hepatotoxic. Here we examined whether the beneficial effects of HyperIL6 could reflect unappreciated competitive inhibition of IL11-dependent IL6ST signaling. In human and mouse hepatocytes, HyperIL6 reduced N-acetyl-p-aminophenol (APAP)-induced cell death independent of STAT3 activation and instead, dose-dependently, inhibited IL11-related signaling and toxicities. In mice, expression of HyperIl6 reduced ERK activation and promoted STAT3-independent hepatic regeneration (PCNA, Cyclin D1, Ki67) following administration of either IL11 or APAP. Inhibition of putative intrinsic IL6 trans-signaling had no effect on liver regeneration in mice. Following APAP, mice deleted for Il11 exhibited spontaneous liver repair but HyperIl6, despite robustly activating STAT3, had no effect on liver regeneration in this strain. These data show that synthetic IL6ST binding proteins such as HyperIL6 can have unexpected, on-target effects and suggest IL11, not IL6, as important for liver regeneration.

## Introduction

The liver has an extraordinary capacity to regenerate in response to injury. Replication of hepatocytes in midlobular zone two underlies liver regeneration (Wei et al., 2021), with a large number of cytokines and growth factors implicated as mitogens (Michalopoulos and Bhushan, 2021). Interleukin 6 (IL6), a member of the larger IL6 family of cytokines, binds with high affinity to its alpha receptor (IL6R) to signal in cis via glycoprotein 130 (gp130; IL6ST) and STAT3. Of all the cytokines implicated in liver regeneration, IL6 is believed to be a predominant auxiliary mitogen (Michalopoulos and Bhushan, 2021; Schmidt-Arras and Rose-John, 2016). This belief is anchored on a seminal study performed in mice globally deleted for Il6, which exhibit reduced STAT3 activity and lesser liver regeneration following injury (Cressman et al., 1996).

It is thought that IL6 can bind to a soluble form of its receptor (sIL6R) to signal in trans to activate IL6 signaling in cells that express IL6ST but low/or no IL6R (Schmidt-Arras and Rose-John, 2016). This led to the design of an artificial fusion protein composed of a truncated form of human IL6R linked to human IL6 (HyperIL6). HyperIL6 stimulates STAT3 signaling up to 1000-fold stronger than the respective separate molecules with high affinity for IL6ST (Fischer et al., 1997; Peters et al., 1998). The HyperIL6 superagonist can reverse fulminant liver failure due to toxin-induced liver damage (Galun et al., 2000; Hecht et al., 2001) and stimulate liver regeneration after partial hepatectomy (Peters et al., 2000). The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has also been observed in the spinal cord (Leibinger et al., 2021), optic nerve (Fischer, 2017), kidney (Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2008), and heart (Matsushita et al., 2005).

We recently found that IL11, a little studied IL6 family protein, is hepatotoxic and important for NASH pathologies (Dong et al., 2021; Widjaja et al., 2019). Furthermore, in a recent study of N-acetyl-p-aminophenol (APAP)-induced liver injury, IL11 was shown to activate NOX4, ERK and JNK and impede liver regeneration (Widjaja et al., 2021). Interestingly, this study demonstrated that synthetic, IL6ST-binding proteins can compete with endogenous IL11 for binding to IL6ST and reduce APAP-induced hepatotoxicity. In light of this new data, it is possible that HyperIL6 could compete with IL11:IL11RA complexes for binding to IL6ST and thus inhibit maladaptive IL11 signaling. Here we investigated whether the mechanism of action of HyperIL6 in liver regeneration is due to inhibition of IL11 signaling and, in contrast to the accepted paradigm, independent of STAT3 activation.

## Results

### STAT-independent HyperIL6 activity inhibits APAP- and IL11-induced hepatocyte cell death

To test our hypothesis, we studied APAP-induced hepatotoxicity. APAP poisoning is a common cause of liver damage, associated with impaired liver regeneration (Bernal and Wendon, 2013). In primary human hepatocytes cultures, incubation with APAP for 24 hr caused cell death in approximately 40% of cells (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B). Inhibition of IL11 signaling using a neutralizing IL11RA antibody (X209) reduced ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activity and cell death (Figure 1A–C). These phenotypes were mirrored by antibody-based neutralization of IL6ST. HyperIL6 also inhibited APAP-induced cell death, and this was associated with increased STAT3 phosphorylation and lesser ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activity (Figure 1A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).

In human hepatocytes, HyperIL6 markedly induced STAT3 phosphorylation but had minimal effect on ERK and no effect on AKT (Figure 1D). Inhibition of IL11 signaling with X209 or anti-IL6ST reduced APAP-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) and maintained cellular glutathione (GSH) levels, which was also true for HyperIL6 (Figure 1E,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C). These initial studies show that HyperIL6 uniquely activates STAT3 but inhibits APAP-induced signaling and cellular phenotypes similarly to neutralizing IL11RA or IL6ST antibodies (Figure 1A–C and E–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

We then examined the functional relevance of HyperIL6-induced STAT3 activation in hepatocytes exposed to APAP. Interestingly, S3I-201 (a STAT3 inhibitor; iSTAT3) had no effect on the protection afforded by HyperIL6 despite inhibiting STAT3 activation (Figure 1A, F and G). Furthermore, S3I-201 had no effect on HyperIL6-induced cell death, ROS induction, or GSH depletion. At the signaling level, S3I-201 inhibited STAT3 activation, but not ERK or JNK phosphorylation nor NOX4 upregulation (Figure 1A–C and E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D). These experiments suggest that the beneficial effects of HyperIL6 are unrelated to STAT3 activity but instead reflect competitive inhibition of IL11 signaling (Figure 1H).

We then examined whether HyperIL6 could directly inhibit IL11 signaling in hepatocytes. Incubation of hepatocytes with IL11 resulted in ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activation and cell death, as expected and similar to that seen with APAP (Figure 1I,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F; Widjaja et al., 2021). HyperIL6 dose-dependently inhibited IL11 signaling and toxicity that was independent of STAT3 phosphorylation and could be titrated away by the addition of soluble IL6ST (sIL6ST) (Figure 1I,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F). We went on to show that the protective effects of HyperIL6 on APAP toxicity in human hepatocytes could be dose-dependently inhibited by the addition of sIL6ST. We confirmed again that the protective effects of HyperIL6 were STAT3 independent and instead related to inhibition of IL11 signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H).

In binding assays, HyperIL6 bound to IL6ST with a similar dissociation constant as an IL11:IL11RA construct (HyperIL11) (KD = 1 nM and 0.95 nM, respectively), whereas IL6 alone did not bind to IL6ST (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C). These data would be consistent with competitive inhibition of endogenous IL11:IL11RA binding to IL6ST by exogenous HyperIL6 and may explain why IL6 alone is ineffective for liver regeneration (Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2011).

### Hepatocyte-specific expression of HyperIL6 prevents APAP-induced liver injury

We next studied the effects of HyperIL6 on APAP-induced liver injury in vivo. Earlier studies used HyperIL6 made from human IL6 and IL6R in the mouse experiments (Galun et al., 2000; Hecht et al., 2001). This could have unappreciated off-target effects, toxicities, and/or immunogenicity issues as human IL6 and IL6R have limited conservation with mouse orthologs (41% and 53.4%, respectively). Therefore, we examined the effects of recombinant mouse HyperIL6 (rm-HyperIL6) versus recombinant human HyperIL6 (rh-HyperIL6) in the mouse model of APAP injury (Figure 2A). We found that both constructs equally reduced serum (alanine transaminase) ALT and (aspartate aminotransferase) AST levels and GSH depletion (Figure 2B–D), activated STAT3, and inhibited ERK and JNK phosphorylation (Figure 2E). Histology showed both constructs also reduced centrilobular necrosis, pathognomonic of APAP liver damage (Figure 2F).

We therefore used species-matched mouse HyperIL6 for hepatocyte-specific HyperIl6 expression studies. Mice were injected with adeno-associated virus serotype 8 (AAV8) encoding either albumin promoter-driven mouse HyperIl6 (AAV8-Alb-HyperIl6) or one of two controls: AAV8-Alb-sIl6st or AAV8-Alb-Null. AAV8-Alb-sIl6st, which encodes mouse sIL6ST, provides a second viral control group while probing for effects of endogenous IL6 trans-signaling. We compared data from the AAV8-treated mice with a group where we inhibited IL11 signaling by X209 (Figure 2G).

The day after APAP (24 hr), mice over-expressing HyperIL6 (Figure 2H) or receiving an anti-IL11RA antibody (X209) had lower ALT/AST levels as compared to AAV8-Alb-Null group (Figure 2I,J). While AAV8-Alb-sIl6st induced high sIL6ST expression, it had no effect on APAP-induced liver injury (Figure 2I–K).

Liver regeneration is associated with a signature of increased Ki67, PCNA, and Cyclin D1 expression (Sekiya and Suzuki, 2011), which was apparent 24 hr post-APAP in both HyperIL6-expressing mice and X209-treated mice but not in AAV8-Alb-Null+ IgG or in sIl6st-expressing mice (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1). HyperIL6 or X209 partially restored liver GSH levels and inhibited ERK and JNK activation, whereas STAT3 was uniquely activated in HyperIL6-expressing mice (Figure 2L,M). Histology revealed typical centrilobular necrosis in APAP-treated AAV8-Alb-Null or sIl6st expressing mice, which was lesser in mice expressing HyperIL6 or following X209 administration (Figure 2N).

These data show that both human and mouse HyperIL6 are protective against APAP-induced liver damage in mice and show that inhibition of IL11 signaling, not activation of STAT3, likely underlies HyperIL6 effects. The data also rule out a pro-regenerative effect of putative endogenous trans-IL6 signaling.

### The protective effects of HyperIL6 on APAP liver injury are STAT3 independent

To exclude a protective role for STAT3 activation downstream of HyperIL6, we first studied the effects of S3I-201 (10 mg/kg) on HyperIL6-mediated hepatoprotection (Figure 3A). Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had reduced serum ALT/AST levels, improved hepatic GSH levels, lesser ERK/JNK activity, and diminished centrilobular necrosis (Figure 3B–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). We observed elevated STAT3 phosphorylation in APAP-treated control mice that was further increased in AAV8-Alb-HyperIl6 mice but absent in mice receiving S3I-201 (Figure 3D). Thus, the beneficial effects of HyperIL6 on hepatoprotection are STAT3 independent at this early time point of assessment.

Markers of liver regeneration peak some 48 hr following liver injury (Michalopoulos and Bhushan, 2021). In addition, APAP liver toxicities can be affected by the administration of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), which we used for S31-201 stock solutions (Park et al., 1988). Therefore, we performed a separate set of experiments to assess regenerative liver phenotypes at 48 hr following APAP and included additional controls to rule out potential confounding effects of DMSO (Figure 3F).

Two days (48 hr) after APAP dosing, APAP and APAP+ DMSO treatment groups were indistinguishable with equally elevated ALT/AST, reduced GSH, activated ERK/JNK, diminished PCNA/Cyclin D1/Ki67, and similar patterns of centrilobular necrosis (Figure 3G–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). Mice receiving APAP plus X209, HyperIL6, or HyperIL6+ iSTAT3 were equally protected from liver damage with lower ALT/AST, higher GSH, and greater expression of PCNA/Cyclin D1/Ki67, while having reduced centrilobular necrosis. At the signaling level, mice receiving APAP plus X209, HyperIL6, or HyperIL6+ iSTAT3 had similarly reduced ERK and JNK signaling. Only mice with HyperIL6 alone had increased STAT3 phosphorylation that was unrelated to the phenotypes studied here (Figure 3G–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). Thus the beneficial effects of HyperIL6 on hepatoprotection and regeneration are STAT3 independent at this later time point of assessment.

Our hypothesis (Figure 1H), and data (Figures 1—3), propose that the beneficial effects of HyperIL6 are due to its inhibition of IL11 signaling. To test this specifically, we injected recombinant mouse IL11 (rmIL11) to mice with HyperIl6 expression± S3I-201 (Figure 3L). Injection of rmIL11 to mice (6 hr) resulted in elevated ALT/AST levels and activation of ERK and JNK, as expected (Figure 3M,N, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Widjaja et al., 2021). Following rmIL11 injection, mice expressing HyperIL6 had elevated STAT3 phosphorylation, lower ALT/AST levels and lesser activation of ERK and JNK, as compared to controls. Administration of S3I-201 to HyperIL6 expressing mice reduced STAT3 activity to baseline but had no effect on its beneficial outcomes at any level of assessment. (Figure 3M,N, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).

### HyperIL6 has no effect on APAP-induced liver injury in mice deleted for Il11

If the protective effects of HyperIL6 are due to its inhibition of IL11 signaling, then HyperIL6 should be ineffective in APAP injury in the absence of IL11. Thus we studied the impact of HyperIL6 on APAP-induced liver injury in mice globally deleted for Il11 (Il11−/−) (Figure 4A; Ng et al., 2021).

APAP dosing resulted in increased IL11 expression in the injured livers of wild-type (WT) mice that was, as expected, absent in Il11−/− mice (Figure 4B). Following APAP, as compared to WT controls, expression of HyperIL6 in WT mice was associated with lesser liver damage and a molecular signature of regeneration (Figure 4B–F). As compared to WT mice receiving APAP, Il11−/− mice dosed with APAP had reduced ALT, AST, and centrilobular necrosis, higher GSH levels along with increased Ki67, PCNA, and Cyclin D1 expression (Figure 4B–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Thus lack of IL11 signaling due to genetic deletion if Il11 stimulates regeneration. Notably, expression of HyperIL6 had no additive effect on hepatoprotection or liver regeneration in Il11−/− mice.

At the signaling level, APAP-related ERK and JNK activation were reduced in both HyperIL6-expressing WT mice and in Il11−/− mice in the absence of HyperIL6 (Figure 4G). While HyperIL6 expression robustly increased STAT3 phosphorylation in both WT and Il11−/− mice, this activity was unrelated to liver protection or regeneration (Figure 4B–G).

### Conclusion

For almost three decades now, IL6 signaling, in particular HyperIL6 activation of STAT3, has been thought to promote liver regeneration (Cressman et al., 1996; James et al., 2003). While some early reports questioned this assertion (Sakamoto et al., 1999), it is now generally accepted (Schmidt-Arras and Rose-John, 2016). Here we show that HyperIL6-mediated inhibition of IL11 signaling (NOX4, ERK, and JNK; Widjaja et al., 2021; Widjaja et al., 2020) in APAP-injured hepatocytes, latent until now, is the dominant mechanism underlying the pro-regenerative effects of HyperIL6 in the damaged liver. We postulate that competition of HyperIL6 with IL11:IL11RA complexes for binding to IL6ST could explain why injection of HyperIL6, but not IL6 itself, promotes liver regeneration (Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2011). Our study suggests that caution is needed when interpreting assumed gain-of-function, on-target effects of synthetic IL6ST-interacting molecules such as HyperIL6, NT-3N (Nishina et al., 2012) or the recently described IC7Fc fusion molecule (Findeisen et al., 2019). IL6ST-related ligand, interacting alpha receptor, and signaling pleiotropy is large, and mechanism of effect is hard to decipher using overexpression of synthetic and alien factors. We end by suggesting IL11 instead of IL6 as a focus for regenerative studies of the liver and perhaps nerves (Fischer, 2017; Leibinger et al., 2021) and kidney (Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2008). With anti-IL11 therapies advancing toward the clinic, this provides interesting opportunities.

### AAV8 vectors

All AAV8 vectors used in this study were synthesized by Vector Biolabs. AAV8 vector carrying mouse HyperIl6 cDNA driven by Alb promoter is referred to as AAV8-Alb-HyperIl6, which was constructed using the cDNA sequences of mouse IL6/IL6R alpha fusion protein (9038 SR, R&D systems). AAV8-Alb-Null vector was used as vector control.

### Cell culture

Primary human hepatocytes (5200, ScienCell) were maintained in hepatocyte medium (5201, ScienCell) supplemented with 2% fetal bovine serum, 1% penicillin-streptomycin at 37°C and 5% CO2. Hepatocytes were serum-starved overnight unless otherwise specified in the methods prior to 24 hr stimulation with different doses of various recombinant proteins as outlined in the main text and/or figure legends. All experiments were carried out at low cell passage (< P3).

### Operetta high-throughput phenotyping assay

Primary human hepatocytes were seeded in 96-well black CellCarrier plates (PerkinElmer) at a density of 5 × 103 cells per well. Following stimulations, cells were incubated 1 hr with 1 µg/ml Hoechst 33,342 (62249, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and DRAQ7 (D15106, Thermo Fisher Scientific) in serum-free basal medium. Each condition was imaged from triplicated wells and a minimum of 23 fields/well using Operetta high-content imaging system 1483 (PerkinElmer). Live and dead cells were quantified using Harmony v3.5.2 (PerkinElmer).

### ROS detection

Primary human hepatocytes were seeded on eight-well chamber slides (1.5 × 104 cells/well). For this experiment, cells were not serum-starved prior to treatment. Twenty-four hours following stimulation, cells were washed, incubated with 25 µM of DCFDA solution (ab113851, abcam) for 45 min at 37°C in the dark, and rinsed with the dilution buffer according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Live cells with positive DCF staining were imaged with a filter set appropriate for fluorescein (FITC) using a fluorescence microscope (Leica).

### Animal models

Animal procedures were approved and conducted in accordance with the SingHealth Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). All mice were housed in temperatures of 21–24°C with 40–70% humidity on a 12 hr light/12 hr dark cycle and provided food and water ad libitum, except in the fasting period, during which only water was provided ad libitum.

### Mouse models of APAP

Prior to APAP, 9–12 weeks old male mice were fasted overnight. Mice were given APAP (400 mg/kg) by intraperitoneal (IP) administration and euthanized 6 hr, 24 hr, or 48 hr post-APAP, as outlined in the main text or figure legends.

### In vivo administration of Rh-HyperIL6, Rm-HyperIL6, or rmIL11

rh-HyperIL6, rm-HyperIL6, or rmIL11 were administered via IP injection at a concentration of 500 µg/kg.

### In vivo expression of HyperIl6 or sIl6st

Six to 8 weeks old male C57BL/6NTac mice (InVivos, Singapore) were injected with 4 × 1011 gc AAV8-Alb-HyperIl6 or AAV8-Alb-sIl6st virus to induce hepatocyte-specific expression of HyperIl6 or sIl6st; control mice were injected with 4 × 1011 gc AAV8-Alb-Null virus. Three weeks following virus administration, mice were given IP administration of APAP and euthanized at the time point outlined in the main text or figure legends.

### In vivo administration of anti-IL11RA (X209) or iSTAT3 (S3I-201)

C57BL/6NTac male mice were IP administered anti-IL11RA (X209, 20 mg/kg), IgG isotype control (11E10, 20 mg/kg), or iSTAT3 (S3I-201, 10 mg/kg) at the beginning of fasting period.

### Il11−/− mice

Mice lacking functional alleles for Il11 (Il11−/−), in which Crispr/Cas9 technique was used to knock out the Il11 gene (ENSMUST00000094892.11), were generated and validated previously (Ng et al., 2021). Six to 8 weeks old male Il11−/− mice and their WT littermates (Il11+/+) were injected with 4 × 1011 gc AAV8-Alb-HyperIl6 virus to induce hepatocyte-specific expression of HyperIl6; control mice were injected with 4 × 1011 gc AAV8-Alb-Null virus. Three weeks following virus administration, mice were given IP administration of APAP and euthanized 24 hr post-APAP.

### Colorimetric assays

The levels of ALT or AST in mouse serum and hepatocyte supernatant were measured using ALT (ab105134, Abcam) or AST (ab105135, Abcam) Activity Assay Kits. Liver GSH measurements were performed using the Glutathione Colorimetric Detection Kit (EIAGSHC, Thermo Fisher). All colorimetric assays were performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol.

### Immunoblotting

Western blots were carried out from hepatocyte and liver tissue lysates. Hepatocytes and tissues were homogenized in radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Thermo Fisher), followed by centrifugation to clear the lysate. Protein concentrations were determined by Bradford assay (Bio-Rad). Equal amounts of protein lysates were separated by SDS–PAGE, transferred to PVDF membrane, and subjected to immunoblot analysis for the indicated primary antibodies. Proteins were visualized using the ECL detection system (Pierce) with the appropriate secondary antibodies.

### Surface plasmon resonance

Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) measurements were performed on a BIAcore T200 (GE Healthcare) at 25°C. Buffers were degassed and filter-sterilized through 0.2 μm filters prior to use. IL6ST was immobilized onto a carboxymethylated dextran (CM5) sensor chip using standard amine coupling chemistry. For kinetic analysis, a concentration series (0.39 nM to 120 nM) of IL6, HyperIL11, or HyperIL6 was injected over the IL6ST and reference surfaces at a flow rate of 30 μl/min. All the analytes were dissolved in HBS-EP+ (BR100669, GE Healthcare) containing 1 mg/ml BSA. The association and dissociation were measured for 210 s and 300 s, respectively. After each analyte injection, the surface was regenerated by two times injection of Glycine-HCl (10 mM, pH 1.5), followed by a 5 min stabilization period. All sensorgrams were aligned and double-referenced. Affinity and kinetic constants were determined by fitting the corrected sensorgrams with the 1:1 Langmuir model using BIAevaluation v3.0 software (GE Healthcare). The equilibrium binding constant KD was determined by the ratio of the binding rate constants kd/ka.

### Histology

#### Hematoxylin and eosin staining

Livers were fixed for 48 hr at room temperature in 10% neutral-buffered formalin (NBF), dehydrated, embedded in paraffin blocks, and sectioned at 7 μm. Sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosineosin (H&E) according to standard protocol and examined by light microscopy.

#### Immuno-histochemistry staining

Livers were processed as mentioned above (H&E staining section). Following dewaxing and antigen retrieval, liver sections were stained with a BOND Polymer Refine Detection Kit (DS9800, Leica) by BOND-III Automated IHC/ISH Stainer (Leica). Ki67 staining was examined by light microscopy.

### Statistical analysis

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software (version 6.07). For comparisons between more than two conditions, one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s correction (when several conditions were compared to one condition) or Tukey’s correction (when several conditions were compared to each other) were used. Comparison analysis for several conditions from two different groups was performed by two-way ANOVA and corrected with Sidak’s multiple comparisons when the means were compared to each other. The criterion for statistical significance was p< 0.05.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.68843.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.68843.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

This paper will have a high impact on the field, as it identifies a new mechanism for the effects of IL6 on liver regeneration and response to injury. The techniques and methodology are also sound and multiple approaches are utilized to answer the main question of the paper.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Overturning the paradigm that IL6 signaling drives liver regrowth while shining light on a new therapeutic target for regenerative medicine" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, including Hossein Ardehali as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #3, and the evaluation has been overseen by Mone Zaidi as the Senior Editor.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions (for the authors):

1) This manuscript can be significantly improved by limiting conclusions of the study to APAP-induced liver injury rather than broad and general conclusions about liver regeneration. Similarly title of the manuscript can be changed to be specific about the APAP liver injury model to avoid misinterpretation.

2) In order to properly study liver regeneration, important time points for peak proliferation such as 48 hr post-APAP should be examined. PCNA western blot should be substantiated with conclusive staining (e.g. Ki67).

3) The findings that protective effects of HyperIL6 against APAP toxicity are Il11 dependent can be substantiated by studies examining if Il11 downstream signaling pathway is activated during APAP toxicity and if it is inhibited by hyperIL6 treatment in vivo. Figure 4 shows effects of HyperIL6 on APAP toxicity in Il11 KO mice, which can be strengthened by examining if Il11 overexpression can overcome hyperIl6 competition and reverse protective effect of HyperIL6 on APAP hepatotoxicity in vivo. Further similar to data in Figure 1i on IL11 toxicity, manuscript can be bolstered by data showing that protective effect of HyperIL6 on APAP toxicity can by titrated away by the addition of soluble gp130.

4) Reference for generation and validation of important mouse strain (Il11 ko) is missing, which should be added. Further, background strain of these mice should be mentioned.

5) The authors assessed ROS production in response to APAP and other reagents in Figure 1. However, no mitochondrial studies are performed. This reviewer is not asking for the mechanism of cellular protection, and agrees with the authors that the paper contains sufficient novelty, but including mitochondrial studies would strengthen the data.

Reviewer Recommendations for the authors:

The paper will have a high impact on the field, as it identifies a new mechanism for the effects of IL6 on liver regeneration. The techniques and methodology are also sound and multiple approaches are utilized to answer the main question of the paper.

1) The major limitation of this study is that the broad conclusion about "overturning the paradigm that Il6 promotes liver regeneration" is not convincingly supported by the presented data. The manuscript is mostly focused on the injury phase of APAP hepatotoxicity (6 and 24 hr post-APAP) and provides limited information on the peak regeneration phase (i.e. later time points – e.g. 48 and 72 hr post-APAP). Further, this is complicated by the fact that liver regeneration in APAP model is a compensatory phenomenon secondary to liver injury. Thus, any effect on liver injury (as observed in this manuscript) will indirectly alter liver regeneration response. Thus, it is hard to interpret about direct role of Il6 in liver regeneration in the current study. Overall, it is incorrect to interpret in general about role of Il6 in regeneration based on the limited data in the APAP model presented in this study. Cleaner model such as partial hepatectomy can be utilized for such interpretations. Further, it will be incorrect to interpret physiological role of Il6 solely based on experiments utilizing HyperIL6 overexpression. In this regard authors should discuss important previous study by James et al. utilizing Il6 KO mice in APAP model which showed that despite no effect on initial APAP-induced liver injury, Il6 KO mice displayed reduced liver regeneration and slower recovery (PMID: 13679052).

2) In Figure 3, in order to demonstrate that protective effects of HyperIL6 are independent of STAT3, authors used STAT3 inhibitor (iSTAT3). Authors investigated only single time point (6 hour post-APAP), which does not provide information if stimulation of liver regeneration by hyperIL6 is independent of STAT3. In order to study liver regeneration, authors should study later time points such as 48 hr post-APAP or at least 24 hr time point as done for other figures in the paper. Further, it is not clear from the manuscript if vehicle control group for iSTAT3 was utilized in this experiment. From in-vitro experiments presented earlier in the manuscript, I assume DMSO was the vehicle for iSTAT3. If that's the case, proper vehicle control is required as DMSO is known to inhibit Cyp2e1 and APAP metabolism to toxic metabolite and thus show protective effects against APAP toxicity.

3) This study does provide interesting data on the role of IL11 in APAP-induced liver injury but with limited mechanistic details. Based on these findings, more comprehensive and mechanistic studies in future will be helpful to delineate how IL11 regulate APAP-induced liver injury. It will also be important to rule out any impact of Il11 deletion on metabolic activation of APAP.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Galun et al., 2000 and Hecht et al., 2001.

claims.claim: HyperIL6 can stimulate liver regeneration after partial hepatectomy.
claims.source: The HyperIL6 superagonist can reverse fulminant liver failure due to toxin-induced liver damage (Galun et al., 2000; Hecht et al., 2001) and stimulate liver regeneration after partial hepatectomy (Peters et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peters et al., 2000.

claims.claim: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has been observed in the spinal cord.
claims.source: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has also been observed in the spinal cord (Leibinger et al., 2021)
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leibinger et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has been observed in the optic nerve.
claims.source: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has also been observed in the spinal cord (Leibinger et al., 2021), optic nerve (Fischer, 2017)
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fischer, 2017.

claims.claim: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has been observed in the kidney.
claims.source: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has also been observed in the spinal cord (Leibinger et al., 2021), optic nerve (Fischer, 2017), kidney (Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2008)
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has been observed in the heart.
claims.source: The pro-regenerative activity of HyperIL6 has also been observed in the spinal cord (Leibinger et al., 2021), optic nerve (Fischer, 2017), kidney (Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2008), and heart (Matsushita et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Matsushita et al., 2005.

claims.claim: IL11 is hepatotoxic and important for NASH pathologies.
claims.source: We recently found that IL11, a little studied IL6 family protein, is hepatotoxic and important for NASH pathologies (Dong et al., 2021; Widjaja et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Dong et al., 2021 and Widjaja et al., 2019.

claims.claim: In APAP-induced liver injury, IL11 activates NOX4, ERK and JNK and impedes liver regeneration.
claims.source: Furthermore, in a recent study of N-acetyl-p-aminophenol (APAP)-induced liver injury, IL11 was shown to activate NOX4, ERK and JNK and impede liver regeneration (Widjaja et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Widjaja et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Synthetic, IL6ST-binding proteins can compete with endogenous IL11 for binding to IL6ST and reduce APAP-induced hepatotoxicity.
claims.source: Interestingly, this study demonstrated that synthetic, IL6ST-binding proteins can compete with endogenous IL11 for binding to IL6ST and reduce APAP-induced hepatotoxicity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by reference to a recent study (Widjaja et al., 2021).

claims.claim: APAP poisoning is a common cause of liver damage, associated with impaired liver regeneration.
claims.source: APAP poisoning is a common cause of liver damage, associated with impaired liver regeneration (Bernal and Wendon, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bernal and Wendon, 2013.

claims.claim: In primary human hepatocytes cultures, incubation with APAP for 24 hr caused cell death in approximately 40% of cells.
claims.source: In primary human hepatocytes cultures, incubation with APAP for 24 hr caused cell death in approximately 40% of cells (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claims.claim: Inhibition of IL11 signaling using a neutralizing IL11RA antibody (X209) reduced ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activity and cell death in APAP-treated hepatocytes.
claims.source: Inhibition of IL11 signaling using a neutralizing IL11RA antibody (X209) reduced ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activity and cell death (Figure 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A–C.

claims.claim: Antibody-based neutralization of IL6ST reduced ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activity and cell death in APAP-treated hepatocytes.
claims.source: These phenotypes were mirrored by antibody-based neutralization of IL6ST.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 1A–C.

claims.claim: HyperIL6 inhibited APAP-induced cell death in hepatocytes, which was associated with increased STAT3 phosphorylation and lesser ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activity.
claims.source: HyperIL6 also inhibited APAP-induced cell death, and this was associated with increased STAT3 phosphorylation and lesser ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activity (Figure 1A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A–C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: In human hepatocytes, HyperIL6 markedly induced STAT3 phosphorylation but had minimal effect on ERK and no effect on AKT.
claims.source: In human hepatocytes, HyperIL6 markedly induced STAT3 phosphorylation but had minimal effect on ERK and no effect on AKT (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Inhibition of IL11 signaling with X209 or anti-IL6ST reduced APAP-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) and maintained cellular glutathione (GSH) levels.
claims.source: Inhibition of IL11 signaling with X209 or anti-IL6ST reduced APAP-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) and maintained cellular glutathione (GSH) levels, which was also true for HyperIL6 (Figure 1E,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: HyperIL6 reduced APAP-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) and maintained cellular glutathione (GSH) levels.
claims.source: Inhibition of IL11 signaling with X209 or anti-IL6ST reduced APAP-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) and maintained cellular glutathione (GSH) levels, which was also true for HyperIL6 (Figure 1E,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: S3I-201 (a STAT3 inhibitor) had no effect on the protection afforded by HyperIL6 in hepatocytes exposed to APAP despite inhibiting STAT3 activation.
claims.source: Interestingly, S3I-201 (a STAT3 inhibitor; iSTAT3) had no effect on the protection afforded by HyperIL6 despite inhibiting STAT3 activation (Figure 1A, F and G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, F and G.

claims.claim: S3I-201 had no effect on HyperIL6-induced cell death, ROS induction, or GSH depletion in APAP-treated hepatocytes.
claims.source: Furthermore, S3I-201 had no effect on HyperIL6-induced cell death, ROS induction, or GSH depletion.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 1A–C and E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: S3I-201 inhibited STAT3 activation, but not ERK or JNK phosphorylation nor NOX4 upregulation in APAP-treated hepatocytes.
claims.source: At the signaling level, S3I-201 inhibited STAT3 activation, but not ERK or JNK phosphorylation nor NOX4 upregulation (Figure 1A–C and E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A–C and E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: The beneficial effects of HyperIL6 are unrelated to STAT3 activity but instead reflect competitive inhibition of IL11 signaling.
claims.source: These experiments suggest that the beneficial effects of HyperIL6 are unrelated to STAT3 activity but instead reflect competitive inhibition of IL11 signaling (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Incubation of hepatocytes with IL11 resulted in ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activation and cell death.
claims.source: Incubation of hepatocytes with IL11 resulted in ERK, JNK, and NOX4 activation and cell death, as expected and similar to that seen with APAP (Figure 1I,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F; Widjaja et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F and citation to Widjaja et al., 2021.

claims.claim: HyperIL6 dose-dependently inhibited IL11 signaling and toxicity in hepatocytes independent of STAT3 phosphorylation.
claims.source: HyperIL6 dose-dependently inhibited IL11 signaling and toxicity that was independent of STAT3 phosphorylation and could be titrated away by the addition of soluble IL6ST (sIL6ST) (Figure 1I,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claims.claim: The inhibitory effects of HyperIL6 on IL11 signaling and toxicity could be titrated away by the addition of soluble IL6ST (sIL6ST).
claims.source: HyperIL6 dose-dependently inhibited IL11 signaling and toxicity that was independent of STAT3 phosphorylation and could be titrated away by the addition of soluble IL6ST (sIL6ST) (Figure 1I,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claims.claim: The protective effects of HyperIL6 on APAP toxicity in human hepatocytes could be dose-dependently inhibited by the addition of sIL6ST.
claims.source: We went on to show that the protective effects of HyperIL6 on APAP toxicity in human hepatocytes could be dose-dependently inhibited by the addition of sIL6ST.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H.

claims.claim: The protective effects of HyperIL6 on APAP toxicity were STAT3 independent and instead related to inhibition of IL11 signaling.
claims.source: We confirmed again that the protective effects of HyperIL6 were STAT3 independent and instead related to inhibition of IL11 signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H.

claims.claim: HyperIL6 bound to IL6ST with a dissociation constant (KD) of 1 nM.
claims.source: In binding assays, HyperIL6 bound to IL6ST with a similar dissociation constant as an IL11:IL11RA construct (HyperIL11) (KD = 1 nM and 0.95 nM, respectively)
claims.evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claims.claim: HyperIL11 bound to IL6ST with a dissociation constant (KD) of 0.95 nM.
claims.source: In binding assays, HyperIL6 bound to IL6ST with a similar dissociation constant as an IL11:IL11RA construct (HyperIL11) (KD = 1 nM and 0.95 nM, respectively)
claims.evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claims.claim: IL6 alone did not bind to IL6ST.
claims.source: In binding assays, HyperIL6 bound to IL6ST with a similar dissociation constant as an IL11:IL11RA construct (HyperIL11) (KD = 1 nM and 0.95 nM, respectively), whereas IL6 alone did not bind to IL6ST (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claims.claim: The binding data would be consistent with competitive inhibition of endogenous IL11:IL11RA binding to IL6ST by exogenous HyperIL6.
claims.source: These data would be consistent with competitive inhibition of endogenous IL11:IL11RA binding to IL6ST by exogenous HyperIL6
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the binding assay data.

claims.claim: The competitive inhibition of IL11:IL11RA binding to IL6ST by HyperIL6 may explain why IL6 alone is ineffective for liver regeneration.
claims.source: These data would be consistent with competitive inhibition of endogenous IL11:IL11RA binding to IL6ST by exogenous HyperIL6 and may explain why IL6 alone is ineffective for liver regeneration (Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the binding assay data and supported by citation to Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Both recombinant mouse HyperIL6 (rm-HyperIL6) and recombinant human HyperIL6 (rh-HyperIL6) equally reduced serum ALT and AST levels in the mouse model of APAP injury.
claims.source: We found that both constructs equally reduced serum (alanine transaminase) ALT and (aspartate aminotransferase) AST levels and GSH depletion (Figure 2B–D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–D.

claims.claim: Both rm-HyperIL6 and rh-HyperIL6 equally reduced GSH depletion in the mouse model of APAP injury.
claims.source: We found that both constructs equally reduced serum (alanine transaminase) ALT and (aspartate aminotransferase) AST levels and GSH depletion (Figure 2B–D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–D.

claims.claim: Both rm-HyperIL6 and rh-HyperIL6 activated STAT3 and inhibited ERK and JNK phosphorylation in the mouse model of APAP injury.
claims.source: We found that both constructs equally reduced serum (alanine transaminase) ALT and (aspartate aminotransferase) AST levels and GSH depletion (Figure 2B–D), activated STAT3, and inhibited ERK and JNK phosphorylation (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Both rm-HyperIL6 and rh-HyperIL6 reduced centrilobular necrosis in the mouse model of APAP injury.
claims.source: Histology showed both constructs also reduced centrilobular necrosis, pathognomonic of APAP liver damage (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Mice over-expressing HyperIL6 had lower ALT/AST levels 24 hr after APAP as compared to AAV8-Alb-Null group.
claims.source: The day after APAP (24 hr), mice over-expressing HyperIL6 (Figure 2H) or receiving an anti-IL11RA antibody (X209) had lower ALT/AST levels as compared to AAV8-Alb-Null group (Figure 2I,J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I,J.

claims.claim: Mice receiving an anti-IL11RA antibody (X209) had lower ALT/AST levels 24 hr after APAP as compared to AAV8-Alb-Null group.
claims.source: The day after APAP (24 hr), mice over-expressing HyperIL6 (Figure 2H) or receiving an anti-IL11RA antibody (X209) had lower ALT/AST levels as compared to AAV8-Alb-Null group (Figure 2I,J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I,J.

claims.claim: AAV8-Alb-sIl6st had no effect on APAP-induced liver injury despite inducing high sIL6ST expression.
claims.source: While AAV8-Alb-sIl6st induced high sIL6ST expression, it had no effect on APAP-induced liver injury (Figure 2I–K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I–K.

claims.claim: Liver regeneration is associated with a signature of increased Ki67, PCNA, and Cyclin D1 expression.
claims.source: Liver regeneration is associated with a signature of increased Ki67, PCNA, and Cyclin D1 expression (Sekiya and Suzuki, 2011)
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sekiya and Suzuki, 2011.

claims.claim: Increased Ki67, PCNA, and Cyclin D1 expression was apparent 24 hr post-APAP in both HyperIL6-expressing mice and X209-treated mice but not in AAV8-Alb-Null+ IgG or in sIl6st-expressing mice.
claims.source: Liver regeneration is associated with a signature of increased Ki67, PCNA, and Cyclin D1 expression (Sekiya and Suzuki, 2011), which was apparent 24 hr post-APAP in both HyperIL6-expressing mice and X209-treated mice but not in AAV8-Alb-Null+ IgG or in sIl6st-expressing mice (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: HyperIL6 or X209 partially restored liver GSH levels following APAP.
claims.source: HyperIL6 or X209 partially restored liver GSH levels and inhibited ERK and JNK activation, whereas STAT3 was uniquely activated in HyperIL6-expressing mice (Figure 2L,M).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L,M.

claims.claim: HyperIL6 or X209 inhibited ERK and JNK activation following APAP.
claims.source: HyperIL6 or X209 partially restored liver GSH levels and inhibited ERK and JNK activation, whereas STAT3 was uniquely activated in HyperIL6-expressing mice (Figure 2L,M).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L,M.

claims.claim: STAT3 was uniquely activated in HyperIL6-expressing mice following APAP.
claims.source: HyperIL6 or X209 partially restored liver GSH levels and inhibited ERK and JNK activation, whereas STAT3 was uniquely activated in HyperIL6-expressing mice (Figure 2L,M).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L,M.

claims.claim: Histology revealed typical centrilobular necrosis in APAP-treated AAV8-Alb-Null or sIl6st expressing mice, which was lesser in mice expressing HyperIL6 or following X209 administration.
claims.source: Histology revealed typical centrilobular necrosis in APAP-treated AAV8-Alb-Null or sIl6st expressing mice, which was lesser in mice expressing HyperIL6 or following X209 administration (Figure 2N).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2N.

claims.claim: Both human and mouse HyperIL6 are protective against APAP-induced liver damage in mice.
claims.source: These data show that both human and mouse HyperIL6 are protective against APAP-induced liver damage in mice
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Inhibition of IL11 signaling, not activation of STAT3, likely underlies HyperIL6 effects on APAP-induced liver damage.
claims.source: These data show that both human and mouse HyperIL6 are protective against APAP-induced liver damage in mice and show that inhibition of IL11 signaling, not activation of STAT3, likely underlies HyperIL6 effects.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: The data rule out a pro-regenerative effect of putative endogenous trans-IL6 signaling.
claims.source: The data also rule out a pro-regenerative effect of putative endogenous trans-IL6 signaling.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had reduced serum ALT/AST levels.
claims.source: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had reduced serum ALT/AST levels, improved hepatic GSH levels, lesser ERK/JNK activity, and diminished centrilobular necrosis (Figure 3B–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had improved hepatic GSH levels.
claims.source: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had reduced serum ALT/AST levels, improved hepatic GSH levels, lesser ERK/JNK activity, and diminished centrilobular necrosis (Figure 3B–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had lesser ERK/JNK activity.
claims.source: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had reduced serum ALT/AST levels, improved hepatic GSH levels, lesser ERK/JNK activity, and diminished centrilobular necrosis (Figure 3B–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had diminished centrilobular necrosis.
claims.source: Following APAP (6 hr), mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, either with or without coadministration of iSTAT3, had reduced serum ALT/AST levels, improved hepatic GSH levels, lesser ERK/JNK activity, and diminished centrilobular necrosis (Figure 3B–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Elevated STAT3 phosphorylation was observed in APAP-treated control mice that was further increased in AAV8-Alb-HyperIl6 mice but absent in mice receiving S3I-201.
claims.source: We observed elevated STAT3 phosphorylation in APAP-treated control mice that was further increased in AAV8-Alb-HyperIl6 mice but absent in mice receiving S3I-201 (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The beneficial effects of HyperIL6 on hepatoprotection are STAT3 independent at 6 hr post-APAP.
claims.source: Thus, the beneficial effects of HyperIL6 on hepatoprotection are STAT3 independent at this early time point of assessment.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Markers of liver regeneration peak some 48 hr following liver injury.
claims.source: Markers of liver regeneration peak some 48 hr following liver injury (Michalopoulos and Bhushan, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Michalopoulos and Bhushan, 2021.

claims.claim: APAP liver toxicities can be affected by the administration of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO).
claims.source: In addition, APAP liver toxicities can be affected by the administration of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), which we used for S31-201 stock solutions (Park et al., 1988).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Park et al., 1988.

claims.claim: Two days (48 hr) after APAP dosing, APAP and APAP+ DMSO treatment groups were indistinguishable with equally elevated ALT/AST, reduced GSH, activated ERK/JNK, diminished PCNA/Cyclin D1/Ki67, and similar patterns of centrilobular necrosis.
claims.source: Two days (48 hr) after APAP dosing, APAP and APAP+ DMSO treatment groups were indistinguishable with equally elevated ALT/AST, reduced GSH, activated ERK/JNK, diminished PCNA/Cyclin D1/Ki67, and similar patterns of centrilobular necrosis (Figure 3G–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G–K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Mice receiving APAP plus X209, HyperIL6, or HyperIL6+ iSTAT3 were equally protected from liver damage with lower ALT/AST, higher GSH, and greater expression of PCNA/Cyclin D1/Ki67, while having reduced centrilobular necrosis at 48 hr post-APAP.
claims.source: Mice receiving APAP plus X209, HyperIL6, or HyperIL6+ iSTAT3 were equally protected from liver damage with lower ALT/AST, higher GSH, and greater expression of PCNA/Cyclin D1/Ki67, while having reduced centrilobular necrosis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 3G–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: At 48 hr post-APAP, mice receiving APAP plus X209, HyperIL6, or HyperIL6+ iSTAT3 had similarly reduced ERK and JNK signaling.
claims.source: At the signaling level, mice receiving APAP plus X209, HyperIL6, or HyperIL6+ iSTAT3 had similarly reduced ERK and JNK signaling.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 3G–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Only mice with HyperIL6 alone had increased STAT3 phosphorylation at 48 hr post-APAP that was unrelated to the phenotypes studied.
claims.source: Only mice with HyperIL6 alone had increased STAT3 phosphorylation that was unrelated to the phenotypes studied here (Figure 3G–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G–K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The beneficial effects of HyperIL6 on hepatoprotection and regeneration are STAT3 independent at 48 hr post-APAP.
claims.source: Thus the beneficial effects of HyperIL6 on hepatoprotection and regeneration are STAT3 independent at this later time point of assessment.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Injection of recombinant mouse IL11 (rmIL11) to mice (6 hr) resulted in elevated ALT/AST levels and activation of ERK and JNK.
claims.source: Injection of rmIL11 to mice (6 hr) resulted in elevated ALT/AST levels and activation of ERK and JNK, as expected (Figure 3M,N, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Widjaja et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3M,N, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and citation to Widjaja et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Following rmIL11 injection, mice expressing HyperIL6 had elevated STAT3 phosphorylation, lower ALT/AST levels and lesser activation of ERK and JNK, as compared to controls.
claims.source: Following rmIL11 injection, mice expressing HyperIL6 had elevated STAT3 phosphorylation, lower ALT/AST levels and lesser activation of ERK and JNK, as compared to controls.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 3M,N, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Administration of S3I-201 to HyperIL6 expressing mice reduced STAT3 activity to baseline but had no effect on its beneficial outcomes following rmIL11 injection.
claims.source: Administration of S3I-201 to HyperIL6 expressing mice reduced STAT3 activity to baseline but had no effect on its beneficial outcomes at any level of assessment. (Figure 3M,N, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3M,N, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: If the protective effects of HyperIL6 are due to its inhibition of IL11 signaling, then HyperIL6 should be ineffective in APAP injury in the absence of IL11.
claims.source: If the protective effects of HyperIL6 are due to its inhibition of IL11 signaling, then HyperIL6 should be ineffective in APAP injury in the absence of IL11.
claims.evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the hypothesis.

claims.claim: APAP dosing resulted in increased IL11 expression in the injured livers of wild-type (WT) mice that was absent in Il11−/− mice.
claims.source: APAP dosing resulted in increased IL11 expression in the injured livers of wild-type (WT) mice that was, as expected, absent in Il11−/− mice (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Following APAP, expression of HyperIL6 in WT mice was associated with lesser liver damage and a molecular signature of regeneration as compared to WT controls.
claims.source: Following APAP, as compared to WT controls, expression of HyperIL6 in WT mice was associated with lesser liver damage and a molecular signature of regeneration (Figure 4B–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B–F.

claims.claim: As compared to WT mice receiving APAP, Il11−/− mice dosed with APAP had reduced ALT, AST, and centrilobular necrosis, higher GSH levels along with increased Ki67, PCNA, and Cyclin D1 expression.
claims.source: As compared to WT mice receiving APAP, Il11−/− mice dosed with APAP had reduced ALT, AST, and centrilobular necrosis, higher GSH levels along with increased Ki67, PCNA, and Cyclin D1 expression (Figure 4B–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Lack of IL11 signaling due to genetic deletion of Il11 stimulates regeneration following APAP.
claims.source: Thus lack of IL11 signaling due to genetic deletion if Il11 stimulates regeneration.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Il11 knockout mice.

claims.claim: Expression of HyperIL6 had no additive effect on hepatoprotection or liver regeneration in Il11−/− mice.
claims.source: Notably, expression of HyperIL6 had no additive effect on hepatoprotection or liver regeneration in Il11−/− mice.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 4B–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: APAP-related ERK and JNK activation were reduced in both HyperIL6-expressing WT mice and in Il11−/− mice in the absence of HyperIL6.
claims.source: At the signaling level, APAP-related ERK and JNK activation were reduced in both HyperIL6-expressing WT mice and in Il11−/− mice in the absence of HyperIL6 (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: While HyperIL6 expression robustly increased STAT3 phosphorylation in both WT and Il11−/− mice, this activity was unrelated to liver protection or regeneration.
claims.source: While HyperIL6 expression robustly increased STAT3 phosphorylation in both WT and Il11−/− mice, this activity was unrelated to liver protection or regeneration (Figure 4B–G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B–G.

claims.claim: HyperIL6-mediated inhibition of IL11 signaling (NOX4, ERK, and JNK) in APAP-injured hepatocytes is the dominant mechanism underlying the pro-regenerative effects of HyperIL6 in the damaged liver.
claims.source: Here we show that HyperIL6-mediated inhibition of IL11 signaling (NOX4, ERK, and JNK; Widjaja et al., 2021; Widjaja et al., 2020) in APAP-injured hepatocytes, latent until now, is the dominant mechanism underlying the pro-regenerative effects of HyperIL6 in the damaged liver.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data and citations to Widjaja et al., 2021 and Widjaja et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Competition of HyperIL6 with IL11:IL11RA complexes for binding to IL6ST could explain why injection of HyperIL6, but not IL6 itself, promotes liver regeneration.
claims.source: We postulate that competition of HyperIL6 with IL11:IL11RA complexes for binding to IL6ST could explain why injection of HyperIL6, but not IL6 itself, promotes liver regeneration (Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a postulate based on the study findings and supported by citation to Nechemia-Arbely et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Caution is needed when interpreting assumed gain-of-function, on-target effects of synthetic IL6ST-interacting molecules such as HyperIL6, NT-3N or IC7Fc fusion molecule.
claims.source: Our study suggests that caution is needed when interpreting assumed gain-of-function, on-target effects of synthetic IL6ST-interacting molecules such as HyperIL6, NT-3N (Nishina et al., 2012) or the recently described IC7Fc fusion molecule (Findeisen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings and supported by citations to Nishina et al., 2012 and Findeisen et al., 2019.

results.result: In primary human hepatocytes, HyperIL6 reduced APAP-induced cell death independent of STAT3 activation by dose-dependently inhibiting IL11-related signaling (ERK, JNK, NOX4) and toxicities. STAT3 inhibition (S3I-201) did not affect HyperIL6's protective effects, indicating that the benefits are unrelated to STAT3 activity but instead reflect competitive inhibition of IL11 signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C32-C42 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (cell death assays, western blots, ROS/GSH measurements, STAT3 inhibitor studies) demonstrating that HyperIL6 protects hepatocytes from APAP toxicity through STAT3-independent inhibition of IL11 signaling. The use of pharmacological STAT3 inhibition (C39-C41) provides strong evidence that STAT3 is not required for HyperIL6's protective effects.

results.result: HyperIL6 dose-dependently inhibited IL11-induced signaling and toxicity in hepatocytes independent of STAT3 phosphorylation. The inhibitory effects could be titrated away by addition of soluble IL6ST (sIL6ST), and sIL6ST could dose-dependently reverse HyperIL6's protective effects on APAP toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47 demonstrate that HyperIL6 directly inhibits IL11 signaling through competitive binding to IL6ST, as evidenced by dose-response experiments and rescue experiments with sIL6ST. The ability of sIL6ST to titrate away HyperIL6's effects provides strong mechanistic evidence for competitive inhibition.

results.result: Surface plasmon resonance binding assays showed that HyperIL6 and HyperIL11 bind to IL6ST with similar dissociation constants (KD = 1 nM and 0.95 nM, respectively), while IL6 alone did not bind to IL6ST. These data are consistent with competitive inhibition of endogenous IL11:IL11RA binding to IL6ST by exogenous HyperIL6.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 provide direct biophysical evidence for the competitive inhibition mechanism through SPR binding assays. The similar binding affinities of HyperIL6 and HyperIL11 for IL6ST, combined with the lack of IL6 binding, support the competitive inhibition model and explain why IL6 alone is ineffective for liver regeneration.

results.result: Both recombinant mouse HyperIL6 (rm-HyperIL6) and recombinant human HyperIL6 (rh-HyperIL6) equally reduced serum ALT/AST levels, GSH depletion, and centrilobular necrosis in a mouse model of APAP injury. Both constructs activated STAT3 and inhibited ERK and JNK phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56, C66 demonstrate that both mouse and human HyperIL6 are protective against APAP-induced liver damage in mice, with consistent effects on multiple injury markers (ALT/AST, GSH, histology) and signaling pathways. This addresses potential concerns about species-specific effects and validates the use of mouse HyperIL6 for subsequent experiments.

results.result: In mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression or receiving anti-IL11RA antibody (X209), APAP-induced liver injury was reduced (lower ALT/AST, restored GSH, reduced necrosis) and liver regeneration markers (Ki67, PCNA, Cyclin D1) were increased at 24 hr post-APAP. Expression of soluble IL6ST (sIl6st) had no effect on APAP-induced liver injury, ruling out a pro-regenerative effect of endogenous IL6 trans-signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C65, C67-C68 provide comprehensive in vivo evidence that HyperIL6 protects against APAP injury and promotes regeneration through inhibition of IL11 signaling rather than activation of IL6 trans-signaling. The negative result with sIL6ST expression (C59) is a critical control that rules out IL6 trans-signaling as the mechanism. The similarity of effects between HyperIL6 and X209 (anti-IL11RA antibody) strongly supports the IL11 inhibition mechanism.

results.result: At 6 hr post-APAP, mice with hepatocyte-specific HyperIL6 expression, with or without STAT3 inhibitor (iSTAT3) coadministration, had reduced serum ALT/AST, improved hepatic GSH, lesser ERK/JNK activity, and diminished centrilobular necrosis. STAT3 inhibition blocked HyperIL6-induced STAT3 phosphorylation but did not affect the protective phenotypes, demonstrating that HyperIL6's hepatoprotective effects are STAT3 independent at this early time point.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 provide strong evidence that HyperIL6's protective effects at 6 hr post-APAP are STAT3 independent through pharmacological STAT3 inhibition experiments. The fact that iSTAT3 blocked STAT3 phosphorylation but not the protective phenotypes is compelling evidence against a STAT3-dependent mechanism.

results.result: At 48 hr post-APAP, mice receiving X209, HyperIL6, or HyperIL6+iSTAT3 were equally protected from liver damage (lower ALT/AST, higher GSH, greater PCNA/Cyclin D1/Ki67 expression, reduced necrosis) with similarly reduced ERK and JNK signaling. Only HyperIL6 alone increased STAT3 phosphorylation, which was unrelated to the phenotypes studied. DMSO vehicle control had no effect on APAP toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 demonstrate that HyperIL6's beneficial effects on hepatoprotection and regeneration are STAT3 independent at 48 hr post-APAP. The inclusion of DMSO control (C77) addresses potential confounding effects of the vehicle used for iSTAT3. The equivalence of effects between X209, HyperIL6, and HyperIL6+iSTAT3 strongly supports the IL11 inhibition mechanism over STAT3 activation.

results.result: Injection of recombinant mouse IL11 (rmIL11) to mice resulted in elevated ALT/AST and activation of ERK and JNK. Mice expressing HyperIL6 had lower ALT/AST and lesser ERK/JNK activation following rmIL11 injection. STAT3 inhibitor (S3I-201) administration to HyperIL6-expressing mice reduced STAT3 activity to baseline but had no effect on HyperIL6's beneficial outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 provide direct evidence that HyperIL6 inhibits IL11-induced liver injury in vivo, independent of STAT3 activation. This experiment directly tests the hypothesis that HyperIL6 acts by inhibiting IL11 signaling and provides strong support for this mechanism.

results.result: In Il11 knockout mice (Il11−/−), APAP dosing resulted in reduced liver damage (lower ALT/AST, reduced necrosis, higher GSH) and increased regeneration markers (Ki67, PCNA, Cyclin D1) compared to wild-type mice, demonstrating that lack of IL11 signaling stimulates regeneration. HyperIL6 expression had no additive effect on hepatoprotection or liver regeneration in Il11−/− mice, despite robustly activating STAT3 in both wild-type and Il11−/− mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C92 provide the most definitive evidence that HyperIL6's protective effects are mediated through IL11 inhibition rather than STAT3 activation. The genetic deletion of Il11 phenocopies HyperIL6's effects, and HyperIL6 has no additional benefit in Il11−/− mice despite activating STAT3. This is a critical experiment that strongly supports the main conclusion of the study.

results.result: The manuscript reviews prior literature establishing that IL6-mediated STAT3 signaling via IL6ST is generally accepted to be beneficial for liver regeneration, and that HyperIL6 (a synthetic IL6:IL6R fusion protein) promotes liver regeneration and has pro-regenerative activity in multiple tissues. This belief is anchored on studies in Il6 knockout mice and experiments showing HyperIL6 can reverse liver failure and stimulate regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C17, C18, C21-C27 accurately summarize the established scientific consensus and prior literature on IL6/HyperIL6 in liver regeneration. These claims are supported by appropriate citations and provide the necessary context for understanding the novelty of the current study's findings.

results.result: The manuscript reviews recent findings that autocrine IL11 activity acts via IL6ST but uses ERK rather than STAT3 to signal, is hepatotoxic, and is important for NASH pathologies. In APAP-induced liver injury, IL11 activates NOX4, ERK, and JNK and impedes liver regeneration. Synthetic IL6ST-binding proteins can compete with endogenous IL11 for binding to IL6ST and reduce APAP-induced hepatotoxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C28-C30 accurately summarize recent findings from the authors' prior work on IL11's role in liver injury. These claims are supported by appropriate citations and provide the rationale for the current study's hypothesis that HyperIL6 may act by inhibiting IL11 signaling.

results.result: The study concludes that synthetic IL6ST binding proteins such as HyperIL6 can have unexpected, on-target effects, and suggests IL11, not IL6, as important for liver regeneration. HyperIL6-mediated inhibition of IL11 signaling is the dominant mechanism underlying its pro-regenerative effects. The authors suggest caution when interpreting effects of synthetic IL6ST-interacting molecules and recommend focusing on IL11 instead of IL6 for regenerative studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C13, C93-C97 represent the main conclusions and implications of the study. These conclusions are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence presented, including in vitro studies, in vivo pharmacological and genetic manipulations, and binding assays. The recommendation to focus on IL11 rather than IL6 for regenerative studies is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: The manuscript provides background information on liver regeneration, IL6 family signaling, HyperIL6 structure, APAP toxicity, and technical considerations for the study (e.g., timing of regeneration markers, DMSO effects, species conservation of IL6/IL6R).
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16, C19, C20, C31, C60, C75, C76, C99 provide accurate background information and technical context for the study. These claims are supported by appropriate citations or represent established knowledge in the field.

results.result: The manuscript notes that anti-IL11 therapies are advancing toward the clinic, providing interesting opportunities for therapeutic development.
results.evaluation: Claim C98 is a factual statement about the current state of anti-IL11 therapy development. While no specific citation is provided, this is consistent with the authors' prior work and represents a reasonable statement about the translational potential of the findings.
